title: Quantum Geometric Friedel Oscillations
authors: Xing-Lei MA, Jinchao Zhao, Bo-Qing Wu, K. T. Law
abstract: In conventional Friedel oscillations, the real-space charge density oscillations induced by an impurity are characterized by an oscillation period set by the Fermi momentum. In this work, we show that the conventional theory is incomplete when the Bloch wavefunctions carry nontrivial quantum geometry. We demonstrate that in metals with an isolated (nearly) flat band at the Fermi energy, quantum geometry induces a distinct type of oscillations, which we call the \emph{quantum geometric Friedel oscillations} (QGFOs). The period of the QGFOs is set by the momentum space separation of the quantum metric hot spots of the flat band. The conventional and quantum metric-induced oscillations coexist at low temperatures. At higher temperatures, the conventional Friedel oscillations away from the impurity site are set by the thermal length such that the oscillations can be easily washed out by temperature effects. Remarkably, the QGFOs decay length is set by the quantum metric length which is defined by the integration of the quantum metric of the flat band. As a result, the QGFOs can persist even at temperatures much larger than the bandwidth of the flat band. Moreover, the decay length is independent of temperature for a wide range of temperatures which is a manifestation of the quantum metric protection. In conclusion, we show that the quantum metric induces novel Friedel oscillations. Our work suggests that the measurement of the QGFOs is a powerful way to detect the quantum metric length (which is associated with the integral of the quantum metric) and the quantum metric hot spot separations (which are associated with the distribution of the quantum metric in the momentum space).
summary: This work introduces Quantum Geometric Friedel Oscillations (QGFOs), showing they arise when the quantum geometry of Bloch wavefunctions is non-trivial. Unlike conventional oscillations whose decay is temperature-sensitive, QGFOs are governed by a robust 'quantum metric length.' Measuring these oscillations provides a novel tool to probe fundamental geometric properties of electronic band structures.
main_problem: The conventional theory of Friedel oscillations is incomplete when considering Bloch wavefunctions with nontrivial quantum geometry, necessitating the characterization of a new oscillation type.
main_result: Quantum Geometric Friedel Oscillations (QGFOs) exist, characterized by a period set by momentum space hot spot separations and possessing a decay length protected by the quantum metric, allowing them to persist at higher temperatures than conventional oscillations.
method: The analysis involves decomposing the total susceptibility into conventional and quantum geometric parts ($\chi_f = \chi^c_f + \chi^g_f$) and calculating the induced density modulation $\deltaho(r)$ using flat-band susceptibility formulas.
model_or_system: The study uses models of metals, specifically focusing on systems exhibiting isolated (nearly) flat bands at the Fermi energy. Calculations are performed using tight-binding models in 1D and 2D lattices.
key_observables: QGFOs (oscillations), quantum metric length ($\ell_{QM}$), momentum space separation of hot spots ($q_G$), and the decay length $\xi$.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$) relative to bandwidth ($W_f$), impurity strength ($U_0$), and topological invariants like the Chern number ($|C|$).
main_assumptions: The theory assumes weak impurities, allowing for certain approximations in the susceptibility calculation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic band structures, real-space density modulations ($\deltaho(x)$) at varying temperatures, and Fourier spectra showing both conventional ($2k_F$) and QGFO peaks. The decay length vs. T plots show a transition from thermal to quantum metric control.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the theoretical gap in conventional theory, then deriving the quantum geometric susceptibility ($\chi^g_f$), demonstrating its distinct characteristics (periodicity $q_G$, temperature-independent decay $\ell_{QM}$), and finally confirming these predictions using 1D and 2D lattice models.
why_interesting: The concept of 'quantum metric protection' suggests a fundamental, geometry-derived robustness in electronic responses that is independent of thermal smearing or simple Fermi surface arguments, which has implications for topological materials physics.
